title: Father, forgive them
hookLine: from the cross: they know not what they do (Luke 23:34)

lines: TWO CRIMINALS, ONE ON EACH SIDE.
cards: Luke's Gospel slows down at the place called Calvary. Two criminals, one on each side. A crowd standing and watching.
And before the soldiers cast lots for his clothes and the mocking that follows, Luke records a sentence from Jesus. It isn't a cry of pain. It isn't a curse.
It's addressed upward, and it's about the people right in front of him. Today: Father, forgive them.

teach.b: First, the line itself. In the King James: "Then said Jesus, Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." Notice the first word.
Father. The same word that opens the prayer Jesus teaches in Luke, said here, of all places. Not judge, not avenger.
The family word, spoken from the worst day. Second, who he forgives. The sentence names no names, and Christians have read it in different ways.
Some hear it about the soldiers carrying out orders. Some widen it to everyone who had a hand in it. Others widen it further still, to every person, themselves included.
The text leaves the circle open, and that openness is part of its force. Third, the reason he gives. For they know not what they do.

teach.h: THEY KNOW WHAT, NOT WHAT IT MEANS.
teach.b: Some readers point out that they know what their hands are doing; what they don't see, in this reading, is what it means: who this is, what it costs, what they've become part of.
Read that way, the line holds two truths at once.
A wrong is happening. And the people doing it don't fully understand it. Forgiveness here doesn't pretend the first truth away.
It leans on the second. Fourth, ordinary life. Sometimes the people who hurt us aren't villains with a plan.
They're tired, scared, careless, following orders, repeating what was done to them.

teach.h: FOR THEY KNOW NOT WHAT THEY DO.
teach.b: They know what they did. They may not see all of what it did. In that gap, between the act and the understanding, this sentence plants itself.
It doesn't make the wrong smaller. It makes room for the person.

how: Christians remember this line among the sayings of Jesus from the cross, read especially on Good Friday, and some churches meditate on the sayings one by one that day.

games.why: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." a prayer, addressed upward, for the people in front of him.

practice: Let one person who wronged you come into view, not to relive it, just enough to see their face, and ask quietly what they didn't understand: what it would cost you, what was happening in them, something they still can't see.
You don't have to excuse them; simply wish them one thing, that someday they see it clearly. If you pray, you can bring them into your prayer with the line from Luke.
